desc:
Encoding. A singly linked list is passed to your function as an array holding the node values from head to tail; an empty array is an empty list. You may build real nodes from it first, or work on the array directly. Lists you return are given as arrays of values from head to tail.

The list is sorted in non-decreasing order. Delete every node whose value occurs more than once, so that only the values that appear exactly once in the original list remain. Return the remaining values from head to tail.

For [1,2,3,3,4,4,5] the answer is [1,2,5]; for [1,1,1,2,3] it is [2,3]. Unlike plain duplicate removal, not even one copy of a repeated value is kept, so the head itself may disappear.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Counting values with a hash map works. Because the list is sorted, you can decide locally instead.

A node is a duplicate if it equals its neighbour. When you find a run of equal values, remove the whole run, including its first node. That needs a pointer to the node before the run, so use a dummy head.

Keep prev (the last kept node). At cur: if cur.next exists and has the same value, remember v = cur.val, skip forward while cur.val == v, then set prev.next = cur. Otherwise prev = cur. In both cases continue from cur (or cur.next in the keep case).
editorial: Use a dummy node before the head. prev always points at the last node that is known to stay. Look at cur = prev.next. If the next node has the same value, the whole run of that value must go: advance cur past every node with that value and link prev.next directly to the first node after the run. Do not move prev yet, because the node after the run can itself start another run of duplicates. If cur is not duplicated, it is kept and prev moves onto it.

Each node is visited a constant number of times: O(n) time, O(1) extra space. The dummy node handles the case where the first value is duplicated. Counting occurrences in a map is also O(n) time but uses O(n) memory and does not exploit sortedness.
